contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: From Vibe Coding to Developing the Company
items.summary: Originally published on yuvalyeret.com . Vibe coding with generative AI. It's the experience of building products in some weird combination of the Las Vegas slot machine with LA's Universal Studios tour. Random, nondeterministic, with a cool product facade with not much behind it. A great way to explore and prototype. Not so much for making real products or capabilities. Spec-driven development came on the scene as the mature version of agentic coding. Specify the feature The idea of spec-driven development is to take an idea, turn it into a specification, and use that specification to guide agentic work. The simplest version of spec-driven development is to use "plan mode", which coding agents now provide. And even the vibe coding platforms such as Base44 and Lovable recommend it as an alternative to one-shotting it. Beyond plan mode you can adopt (or make) a harness that explicitly defines the workflow, policies, handoffs, and agent responsibilities. Think GitHub's Spec Kit, Every's Compound Engineering, Amazon's Kiro, etc. Specify how we work here Each one of these frameworks/harnesses provides an opinionated view on what an agentic workflow should look like. Or, in other words, a specification for how to do development. That specification drives the agentic software workflow, also known as the agentic software factory. It brings predictability through guardrails that steer agents. Kind of like how processes steer humans working together. Each of these frameworks comes with a starter definition of workflow. Using it effectively requires continuously adapting it to your own world. It's like Scrum's Definition of Done or Kanban's definition of workflow. Don't expect spec-driven-development harnesses to provide a full recipe for how to work in your world. Use them as frameworks which you use, inspect, and adapt. What does "adapt" look like? Making changes in the configuration files that agents refer to as they drive work throughout the software factory. Think AGENTS.md, constitution.md, skills, and LangGraph loop configuration. This becomes our operating system manifested as version-controlled code. So why does spec-driven development feel like babysitting AI agents? Even in spec-driven development, you can feel reduced to approving individual steps for the agents, constantly bombarded with walls of Markdown. Maybe you aren't coding, but you have to review the large code PRs. That's not exactly the vision of the agentic software factory we were sold on, is it? Wouldn't it be nice if we could indeed "vibe code" through a trusted software factory? To be able to express what we want, and get working high-quality software at the other end that achieves the outcome we are looking for? The idea is to "one-shot" a trusted agentic loop. And get a higher-quality, more predictable result even when it's nondeterministic LLMs executing the loop. It's not that dissimilar from a human-powered software factory. Humans aren't deterministic either. And when they're doing high-level knowledge work such as software development there's plenty of variability. Agile/Flow-based ways of working are designed to bring discipline and predictability into the nondeterministic world of R&D. That doesn't mean everything we build will work. It doesn't mean everything will be useful. It means we are optimizing the performance of the design factory to maximize our ability to turn human talent and capacity into useful products or capabilities. And in the agentic age, we are optimizing the performance of both human capacity and AI tokens, through continuously tinkering with the operating system/process that we refer to when doing work in the factory. You've sampled it and run it multiple times. Sometimes it will fail, and you have a process for fixing it. You are accountable for what the agents are doing. View full-size diagram Trustable output is still output Even if we created an efficient software factory, that's only part of the journey. Delivering software doesn't necessarily mean customers adopt it. It doesn't necessarily mean we've delivered value. The impact comes from software that enables new behaviors for our customers. Effective agency depends on alignment to what we're trying to do. Before giving agents the keys to choose features, improve the outcome orientation of the agents and their harness. Otherwise, they're going to build junk. It might work, but it might not move the needle in any meaningful way. For years I've worked with organizations that call themselves product organizations with feature teams and cross-functional teams. When you look at the actual work, very few teams are really empowered to own end-to-end outcomes. Most of the work requires handoffs and waiting, with dependencies everywhere. If you want agency, even for humans, you need to create the right structure. Focus on smaller bets that involve fewer teams. Reshape the teams to localize collaboration and coordination. items.title: Stop Demoing Your AI Rollout. Find the Unavoidable Project.
items.summary: Originally published on yuvalyeret.com . What a developer sees when the AI coding CLI rollout arrives From everybody’s perspective, if I’m a developer on a team, it’s not unavoidable right now. I don’t really have to use it right now. I can keep on developing. And at some point, somebody might tell me you have to use it. If I’m told I have to use it, then that’s the only reason I do it. Because it’s mandated. And I still don’t feel the pull. How will that resistance manifest itself? I’ll just use tokens: I’ll use it, I’ll do some demo, but I won’t really believe in it. I’ll go through the motions. Isn’t a mandate the only thing that gets people to move? One path that leaders often take is to follow initial promising results with a mandate to follow new ways of working throughout the organization. This brute force approach can work in some environments but more often stalls. One frustration is that if you don’t mandate, people don’t change. A lot of the things that I do is to take concepts that people use in other domains and apply them to change management. In the world of product, you cannot really push a product. You can try, but people buy when there’s pull. What does that mean? People buy your product when there’s something that they’re trying to do that’s unavoidable right now, and the options they look into are lacking. They look at options, and they only find lacking options. When that’s the case, they will pull from you, whether you are the transformation consultant on the outside that’s selling services, or a transformation coach on the inside, trying to sell change. Change is a Product . It should be customer-centric, designed for the context. As long as the transformation you’re trying to “market/sell” internally is nice to have, you’re not going to have much success. You will be stuck in the “pain cave” , struggling to convince people to transform and tempted to use brute force. Stop giving demos and go find the unavoidable project Giving demos is not gonna get people to change. One of the things that Rob Snyder says is you can’t sell a product by demo. Product demos are a waste of time. Our role as change agents is to assess pull, and to create pull. You need to find what are the unavoidable projects that your product will help people do. You need to find the people that have an unavoidable project that they cannot currently do well. I couldn’t care less about proving the concept. It’s not about the solution. It’s about: do people have a problem that they need this for? So what are the examples of pull that did happen? What are the case studies? Was it a feature that we needed to develop very fast? What couldn’t we do without AI? Find the case studies inside the organization where the transformation addressed a must-have to-do list item. Use these case studies to sell/market the transformation and look for similar opportunities where it could potentially be a must-have. Who your early adopters actually are Some people are early adopters, the way they’re wired. There are the innovators, the people that will do something just because it’s new. The early adopters are different. The early adopters are exactly the people that have pull. They have such a big problem that they’ll be willing to use your product even though it sucks. Not because they’re willing to try new things. It’s a combination of: they’re willing to try new things, and they have an unavoidable project that they don’t have a good solution for. So they’re already doing some things that are workarounds. This would actually make their life better. Every time you’re trying to drive a product to market, that’s the first group that you need. And if there’s no problem in the audience, you have no chance. Why “let’s do it for everybody” backfires In order to cross the chasm between these early adopters and the early majority, that needs proof and proper solutions, there’s a whole body of work on a full kit. That’s where you need the playbook. That’s where you need to show successes from others. Show the small wins. But it doesn’t make sense to try and cross the chasm before you get to zero to one. To initial product-market fit. So it’s different stages of the product life cycle. And a lot of the time in organizational transformation, we’re just saying, yeah, let’s do it for everybody. If you force a solution that is not ready for the mainstream, you kill its credibility. What if AI really is unavoidable for everyone? I agree that at some point, the organization will create the context where people will understand: jump on the AI wagon, or you don’t have a role in the industry. Like, it’s happening, it’s unavoidable. You need to learn how to work with AI. But it might be the case that people actually have pull right now, and they’re refusing the CLI because it really sucks. It’s hard to use. So maybe if the solution gets improved a bit, we’ll be able to serve this pull. I know the dynamics of what the developers are really saying and where…

items.title: Great Project Managers Make Great Scrum Masters
items.summary: Image I’ve been using Scrum for over 20 years now. And great Scrum Masters can come from anywhere. They can be people from the business, Developers, HR Managers, and (occasionally) Leadership. But I often see Scrum Masters come to Scrum from Project Management. It makes sense. There is a lot of overlap. Project Managers facilitate meetings, help a team deliver value, remove impediments, and escalate risks. But there is also a lot that Project Managers need to let go of in order to be great Scrum Masters. Among other things, they need to let go of creating the plan for how the work will get done - that belongs to the Developers, and they create their plan every Sprint. And they need to let go of owning the Scope and timeline - those belong to the Product Owner, and Project Managers can coach them in how to create an effective timeline and how to use that to make better decisions on what Scope is most important. The core skills for a Scrum Master have strong overlap with Project Management. Communication, leadership, facilitation, impediment removal, focus and team building skills are all important to the Scrum Master. Here are ten reasons why I think Project Managers can make great Scrum Masters. They already remove obstacles. Great Project Managers care about clearing the path so the team can move forward. That instinct maps directly to the Scrum Master’s job of removing impediments. They’re comfortable escalating when needed. They know when an issue is bigger than the team and needs organizational attention. A good Scrum Master does the same — without turning every issue into a status report to management. They know how to bring the right people together. They understand who needs to be in the room and how to keep the conversation focused. Facilitation is one of the core skills of an effective Scrum Master. They pay attention to whether work is actually progressing. They’re not satisfied with activity. They want to see movement toward a goal. That focus on outcomes serves a Scrum Master well. They help groups stay focused on a goal. Even though the Product Owner owns the Product Goal and the ordering of the backlog, the ability to help a team maintain focus is valuable in every Scrum event. They are used to managing risk and uncertainty. Complex work always involves unknowns. Experienced Project Managers already live in that space. Scrum simply gives them a more empirical way to handle it. They understand stakeholder dynamics. They know how to communicate progress, surface concerns, and keep stakeholders informed without over-controlling the conversation. That skill helps when coaching the organization in Scrum. They value clear (and hopefully brief) communication. Whether it’s a status update or a difficult conversation, strong Project Managers know how to make information transparent. Transparency is one of the three pillars of empiricism. They are used to serving multiple groups at once. Project Managers often coordinate across teams, departments, and leaders. Scrum Masters do similar work when they help the wider organization adopt Scrum and remove cross-team impediments. They already practice versions of servant leadership. The best Project Managers I know don’t succeed by commanding. They succeed by enabling. That orientation is the foundation of great Scrum Mastery. A great Scrum Master does not own the plan or assign the work. They create the conditions for the team to come up with their own plan, and they help them execute it. They facilitate, coach, and remove impediments. They help the team inspect and adapt. The best project managers already practice versions of this, even inside traditional environments. Conclusion Project Managers who want to transition to the Scrum Master role - or even who want to use Scrum to deliver their projects or help lead an Agile transformation to a product structure - should play to their strengths but also learn the structure of Scrum. I suggest Project Managers should invest time in the Applying Professional Scrum class or the Professional Scrum Master class with Rebel Scrum to get a better understanding of how to use Scrum to deliver value. If you have a whole team who is moving to Scrum, it is ideal if they can take the Applying Professional Scrum class together to level-set on expectations and make the transition to Scrum as smooth as possible. Project Managers who cling to control struggle in the Scrum Master role. They become bottlenecks or gatekeepers. The ones who succeed are the ones who already suspected that controlling every detail was not the highest-leverage use of their time. Using Scrum can help Project Managers to empower teams and maximize value for the organization.

items.title: How To Create The First Version Of Your Definition of Done
items.summary: Image Done is a simple yet mysterious concept. Ask different Developers when a Product Backlog Item is Done, and you'll get different answers, a serious problem that costs the team transparency. On the other hand, every Sprint is a learning loop, and the Scrum Team should close that loop by creating a Done Increment, delivering it to Stakeholders, and gathering their feedback. If you don't create a Done Increment each Sprint, you don't close the learning loop. That's how important Done is. In fact, if we had to squeeze Scrum into a single sentence, it would be: "Create a Done Increment each Sprint." But why is Done usually overlooked? Because there's a big difference between a feature working and a feature being Done. Many people see these as identical, but they are not. Done is a much broader umbrella than merely working. Imagine one of the expectations in your Definition of Done is: "Code coverage is at least 70%." You've finished coding and your feature works, but it isn't Done yet if it doesn't meet that 70% threshold. The lesson: a feature can work and still not be Done. Conversely, when a feature is Done, it necessarily works. Let’s see what the Scrum Guide says about the Definition of Done: The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. What is an Increment? Many people have problems with the definition of the Increment. Let’s explore it. Scrum is based on iterative development and incremental delivery. The Increment is like a container. You always have just one Increment, and when a Product Backlog Item is built, it is added to the Increment, making it bigger. So, over time, your Increment gets bigger and bigger. See this image: Image Scrum Guide introduces Increment this way: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. The big message The Definition of Done is on the Increment (Product) level, not on the Feature level. Whatever you have on the feature level is Acceptance Criteria, not Definition of Done. So, for one product you have just one Definition of Done, and for each feature you have one Acceptance Criteria. How to build the Definition of Done? This is the whole Scrum Team’s accountability to build a DoD. There are seven categories of expectations that you need to consider when you want to create DoD as follows: Process Expectations Technical Expectations Delivery Expectations Industry Standards Organization Expectations Non-Functional Requirements AI Impact Expectations (If you are using AI to build the product) You need to sit with your Scrum Team and go through the 7 categories one by one and decide what expectations you want to have in your Definition of Done for each category. Bear in mind, DoD is a live concept, meaning it evolves over time as the team learns more. Don’t make it big or difficult to adhere to. Start with a lightweight version. In the first step, the main goal is that Developers learn to completely adhere to the Definition of Done and use it in their day-to-day work. It means that after completion of building a Product Backlog Item, they open their DoD checklist and go through all the items, and when all of them get a checkmark, they claim their PBI is Done. This behavior is a fundamental and crucial one for the success of the Scrum Team. Focus on building this behavior in your Scrum Team until you see they automatically use the DoD. items.title: When AI Suggests a Pattern in Customer Feedback, What Might Be Missing?
items.summary: AI can help Product Owners identify patterns in customer feedback. Understanding what those patterns mean often requires hearing from people whose experiences are missing from the original reports. Choosing whom to speak with next can make a real difference to the next product decision. Image Consider, for example, a service that allows customers to book repair appointments. Several customers have contacted support because they struggled to find a suitable appointment. An AI tool groups these reports together, bringing a possible pattern to the Product Owner's attention. The reports suggest a problem with the booking experience. The Product Owner might consider improving the appointment search or changing how available appointments are displayed. Before deciding where to invest the Scrum Team's effort, however, it would be useful to understand whose experiences the reports represent and what other information could help explain the problem. Look beyond the initial feedback The support reports provide information about customers who encountered difficulties and decided to contact support. Other customers may have abandoned the booking process without reporting anything, while some may have completed their bookings despite experiencing similar difficulties. These different experiences are relevant because the same complaint can have several explanations. Customers might struggle to understand the search results, or the available appointments might simply be unsuitable for their needs. Each explanation could lead to a different product decision. AI can help us investigate these possibilities by comparing feedback with other available information. For example, the Product Owner could use AI to explore patterns in anonymized booking data alongside the support reports. If many customers leave after viewing appointment availability, that could reveal a group whose experiences are worth investigating. The data would help identify where customers leave the process, while conversations could help us understand why. Together, these sources provide a better starting point for deciding what to investigate. Talk to people who could challenge your assumptions When several customers report the same difficulty, speaking with more people who have raised similar complaints may seem like a sensible next step. Those conversations can provide valuable detail, but they may also reinforce an interpretation based on a limited group of customers. During a feedback session I attended, frequent users suggested improvements to search filters and ways to complete bookings faster. One participant who had been relatively quiet raised a different concern. She sometimes hesitated before confirming a reservation because she was unsure whether she could change or cancel it later. Her concern highlighted a different obstacle to completing a booking, one that the other suggestions had overlooked. The same reasoning applies to our repair-appointment example. Based on the information gathered so far, a useful next step could be to speak with customers who recently searched for an appointment but left without completing a booking. Their experiences might help us understand whether the difficulties reported to support reflect a broader problem. In qualitative research, this approach is related to purposeful sampling , which involves selecting participants whose experiences can provide useful information about a particular question. Some approaches deliberately seek cases that challenge an emerging explanation, helping researchers examine its limitations [2]. AI can support the selection process by helping us examine where information is missing and which customer groups might offer a different perspective. The Product Owner can then decide whom to approach, taking into account the available evidence and appropriate permissions for contacting customers. Use the conversation to understand the problem Once we have identified a relevant customer group, the next step is to understand their experience. For someone who abandoned the booking process, we might ask: "Can you walk me through what happened when you were looking for an appointment and decided to stop?" We could then explore what the customer expected to happen and how they continued with their repair. The conversation may reveal difficulties with the search interface or limitations in appointment availability. Depending on what emerges, the Scrum Team might also examine usage data or observe how customers interact with the product. A few conversations can help clarify an uncertainty and guide further investigation. Understanding how widespread a problem is may require additional evidence. items.title: 10 Reasons Why I Love Scrum
items.summary: Image Every once in a while, I'll read another article declaring that Scrum is dead. But when I look at the reasons, I often find that the problem isn't Scrum at all. It's that the team isn't using Scrum effectively in the first place. And ironically, the cure is often to use Scrum to improve how you're using Scrum! For example, one common complaint is that Scrum involves too many meetings. Well, that's a great topic for your next Sprint Retrospective! Another complaint is that teams can't get anything Done within a Sprint. That might be a sign of organizational impediments that need to be addressed, or that the team needs to break work into smaller, more manageable pieces. These aren't necessarily reasons to abandon Scrum. They're opportunities to improve. I've spent more than 20 years working with IT teams to deliver value. And in my experience, many of the teams with the highest morale, the best attitudes, and the strongest outcomes have one thing in common: Scrum. So, despite all the articles declaring its demise, I'm still a fan. Here are ten reasons why I love Scrum. 1) Less time in meetings. Image Scrum provides just enough structure to help teams spend less time in meetings. That's right. I said less time. There's a common myth that Scrum teams spend all their time in meetings. I understand why people think that. Scrum does require several events, but each has a specific purpose and a timebox. These aren't meetings for the sake of meetings. They're essential opportunities for collaboration. Here's what I mean. Let's say your team uses two-week Sprints. At Sprint Planning , the team decides what to accomplish during the Sprint and creates a plan for delivering it. Every day, the Developers spend no more than 15 minutes in the Daily Scrum inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting their plan. At the end of the Sprint, the team and stakeholders inspect the results and discuss what to do next at the Sprint Review . Then, during the Sprint Retrospective , the Scrum Team identifies ways to improve. Throughout the Sprint, the team also refines the Product Backlog as needed. When you list everything out, it might sound like a lot. But these events replace many unnecessary status meetings and last-minute emergency discussions. The team plans together, checks progress regularly, reviews results, and continuously improves. When Scrum is used effectively, teams spend less time in meetings because they address problems early instead of kicking the can down the road. 2) Role clarity. Image Image credit: Office Space (1999), © 20th Century Fox. People work better when they understand what's expected of them. One of the things I love about Scrum is how clearly it defines accountabilities. The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product. They establish a Product Goal and order the Product Backlog so the team knows what's most important. Imagine the product is a home renovation. The Product Backlog might include replacing the kitchen countertops, updating the flooring, and repainting the living room. The Product Owner determines which improvements are most valuable and sets the direction for the team. The Developers are accountable for creating a usable Increment each Sprint. In our home renovation example, they're like the contractors doing the work. They decide how to organize the work, who will tackle which tasks, and how much they can realistically accomplish. Developers also provide valuable feedback. For example, if the Product Owner wants glitter in the paint, the Developers might explain why that's a terrible idea! They bring their expertise to the conversation while the Product Owner remains accountable for product value. Finally, the Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and improving the Scrum Team's effectiveness. They help everyone understand Scrum, support self-management, help remove impediments, and ensure Scrum events are positive, productive, and kept within their timeboxes. Everyone knows their accountability, and everyone contributes to the team's success. That's a powerful combination. 3) It uncovers all the crummy processes. Image Scrum has a way of exposing inefficient processes. Fast. Because Scrum Teams must create a usable, Done Increment every Sprint, anything slowing them down becomes difficult to ignore. For example, a traditional project team might tolerate a cumbersome change-control process for years. A Scrum Team trying to deliver value every Sprint quickly discovers just how much that process gets in the way. The Scrum Master helps the team address these impediments, working with leadership when necessary to make organizational processes more effective and lightweight. This can make adopting Scrum uncomfortable at first. Suddenly, problems that everyone has learned to live with are out in the open. But that's a good thing! Fixing those problems doesn't just help the Scrum Team. It can improve how the entire organization operates.…

items.title: Four ways pharma companies actually adopt agility
items.summary: Image In the first post of this series , I suggested replacing "should we introduce agile?" with three other questions: agile to solve what, where and how much, and what kind. Another question I'm sometimes asked is: "So what are other pharma companies actually doing?" If you work in this industry, you know it's a relatively closed circle of large companies with many links between them: they co-promote drugs together, and their people often move from one company to another. So it's natural to be curious about what the others are doing. Two questions that sort most cases One imperfect but useful way I have found to describe how a pharma company is adopting agile ways of working is to use two dimensions. The first is how deliberately the company is pursuing agility . At one end, the change is organic: a team (sometimes in R&D, sometimes in marketing) tried Scrum, it helped, and the neighbours noticed. Or agility emerges as a by-product of other changes that nobody labelled "agile". At the other end, someone with authority (the CEO, or the head of a particular therapeutic area) decided on purpose to make the organization more agile, with sponsorship, budget and a plan. The second dimension is how wide it is . Is it one team, one function, or the whole company? Put those two questions on two axes and you get four patterns. Image You'll notice the bottom-right corner is shaded. Enterprise-wide change that nobody decided on virtually never happens in pharma: budgets, governance and HR processes don't change by word of mouth. Grassroots A team in early research, IT or a new business unit starts using Scrum or Kanban on its own. It helps. Neighbouring teams notice and copy what they see. There is no formal program and no budget line; it spreads mostly by word of mouth. The strength of this pattern is real ownership: nobody is doing it because they were told to. Its limit is that it usually hits a ceiling at the edge of the team. Budgets, goal-setting, HR processes and governance stay the same, so the teams end up working one way inside a system that expects another. It also depends heavily on a few enthusiasts, and it can fade when they move on. Function-led transformation One department invests deliberately: the commercial organization, medical affairs, or a digital and data function. It has a sponsor, a budget and a plan. Other functions remain traditional. In my experience, this is often where things start. The strength is a sponsor with real authority over a clear scope, which makes results visible and decisions possible. The limit shows up at the interfaces. A commercial team working in short cycles still depends on functions that plan once a year, approve in sequence, or measure success differently. Much of the friction, and much of the value left on the table, sits in those handoffs. Operating model redesign Here the company is deliberate about change, but not about agility. Nobody announces an agile transformation. Instead, governance, planning cadence, team structures and decision rights are adjusted one piece at a time, often as part of a DX strategy or a broader reorganization. Each change is decided; the overall shift toward agility is not. It emerges from the accumulation. The strength is that it works on the structures that usually block agility, and it avoids the fatigue some people feel about the agile label. The limit is that without a shared vocabulary and a clear "why", it can turn into a series of reorganizations that people experience as change for its own sake. Enterprise program Top-down and sponsored by the C-suite, often with a shared framework for teams (e.g. Scrum), enterprise-level processes (e.g. QBR), a new organizational structure, and a dedicated transformation office. In pharma, I have seen this pattern a couple of times. When leadership truly owns it, the strength is alignment and momentum: everyone hears the same message and the same vocabulary at the same time. The limit is the risk of a big-bang, one-size-fits-all rollout. As we saw in the first post, a single pharma company spans very different kinds of work, and one playbook rarely fits all of them. Most companies are in several boxes at once As much as I find it useful to sort adoption patterns on the above two axes, many large pharma companies don't sit in only one of these boxes. They can exhibit several patterns at the same time, with different functions, or different therapeutic areas, at different stages of adoption and intentionality. It's quite common to find, in the same company, a couple of autonomous Scrum teams in early research, a commercial organization in the middle of a deliberate transformation, and a DX program led by the IT department, trying to redesign governance. And each one can be managed surprisingly independently. In addition, the patterns move over time. For example, a couple of successful Scrum teams can pave the way for an operating model redesign. items.title: From Babysitting AI to Developing the Factory
items.summary: Originally published on yuvalyeret.com . "I feel like I'm constantly babysitting agents who throw walls of markdown and code at me," shared a senior engineer I've been coaching through AI adoption. He was missing the joy of troubleshooting tough problems himself. This frustration reminded me of my days troubleshooting Linux kernel issues. The friction, challenge, and joy when you eventually find that sneaky memory leak or kernel oops. Where does that joy come from when agents do the coding? I see signs of this in myself too: fatigue from the volume of content agents pour on us, whether code, text or messages. Working more with AI should allow us to be in flow more, with fewer meetings and interruptions. But something in the way we work with AI is not getting us there. Spec-driven development is intended to be a step forward from vibe coding, but I hear more and more of engineers who feel reduced to approving individual steps in the workflow. It seems like the power of agentic development is being neutered, and engineers are caught in the middle. Full gas in neutral So we let the agents take a step in the spec-driven workflow. What do we do meanwhile? We can't idle. And we have tokens to max out. So we spawn a new agent to work on a new thing. But then the original agent comes back with a question or a wall of markdown for us to review. Pretty soon the agent threads pile on and on. And you, the human, spend more and more time context switching and less and less time in the flow zone. Which also leads to burnout. Can you injure yourself making software using AI? Joshua Kerievsky's seminal article on #techsafety talks about common injuries to software makers. The way we currently make stuff with AI is prone to many of these injuries e.g. fractured flow, merge misery, brain hernia. From injury risk to becoming a remedy How can we shift AI coding from being a cause of injury to makers, to being a remedy to some of these common injuries? That's what I'm exploring in my coaching conversations. And this shift requires engineers and their leaders to shift their perspective. From making software features to making software factories. My advice to the frustrated burned-out engineer was to start looking at AI prompts and loops as source code in their own right. And to take on the challenge of turning this into something they enjoy working with, where they feel that Claude works for them, not vice versa. It's about regaining our human agency using agentic AI. From developing features to developing the software factory - in practice An agent makes a decision we don't like, and we find it in the code review or the spec review. One option is to override it: include this requirement in the spec, include this intent, use this pattern in the code. Change this, change that. What we need to look at is the system that made this decision. The software factory needs to be designed for the limitations and capabilities of the coding agents, with the right guardrails. When a rule isn't having the intended effect, treat it as a bug. Create an evaluation or a test that proves it, then work on it through test-driven development. Improve the skills, improve the context, improve the system that creates the code, and then rerun and see if it's better. If “humans make the decisions” means humans decide how to code something, we're back to humans reviewing all the code. There are also decisions about what's important: choosing the feature, the architecture, the outcome, the system behavior we want to see. In my conversation with Shay Mandel at Next Insurance , he put it this way: “We are not the initial reviewer. We are the last reviewer.” The human is reviewing work that agents deem "Done". And the expectation is that over time, these reviews come up with fewer and fewer findings. How? By fixing the factory so that it can find and fix the finding itself, or ideally build quality in from the get-go. Let's say you're reviewing a draft PR. Instead of asking an agent to fix the findings, work with it to fix the specification of the factory (whether that's agents.md, constitution or skill files), and then use the draft PR and the finding as a "specification by example" of what it should be able to find itself as part of its workflow, as well as consider when it is specifying and planning to avoid in the first place. You can then either move on to the next thing you're working on and see if it does better, or ask the agent to repeat the whole workflow using its new factory version and evaluate whether it's indeed building quality in. Once you get to the point where what the agentic workflow considers good quality meets your own criteria, you can start trusting it more and more. This is the point where human in the loop can start to shift towards human on the loop. items.title: So bringen Sie KI-Initiativen über den Proof of Concept hinaus
items.summary: Ursprünglich veröffentlicht auf yuvalyeret.com. Wo sterben KI-Initiativen eigentlich? Ich bin versucht zu sagen, dass ein KI-natives CRM, bei dem die Verkäufer die Informationen nicht manuell eingeben müssen, großartig ist. Jeder wird das lieben. Aber ich habe so oft erlebt, dass selbst diese offensichtlichen Annahmen irgendwann scheitern. Wie oft denken wir, dass Dinge wirklich wünschenswert sind, ein Feld voller Träume, in das die Menschen wirklich kommen werden, und springen dann auf die technologische Machbarkeit? Wollen wir selbst großartige Ideen testen? Und wie testet man so etwas, ohne es in der KI-Welt zu bauen? Wird es tatsächlich irgendjemand wollen, wenn Sie es gebaut haben? Clemens Adolphs, Mitbegründer von AIce Labs, in unserem Gespräch „Skalieren mit Agilität“: Bei allem, was Sie jemals bauen, besteht im Großen und Ganzen ein Marktrisiko: Wird es irgendjemand tatsächlich wollen, wenn Sie es einmal gebaut haben? Und Marktrisiko muss nicht zwangsläufig bedeuten, dass man ein verbraucherorientiertes Produkt entwickelt und dieser es kaufen muss. Es könnte sich auch einfach um ein internes Tool handeln, das Sie einführen und das Ihre Mitarbeiter nutzen sollen, aber sie nutzen es nicht. Es gibt zu viel Reibung. Sie möchten einfach lieber aus ChatGPT kopieren und einfügen, als sich durch Ihre fünf internen Ebenen zu klicken. Zu seinem letzten großen Projekt: Sagen wir, das letzte große Projekt: Es hatte bereits eine gewisse interne Validierung, weil sie über ein grundlegendes Tool verfügten, das die Sache erledigte und angenommen wurde. Wenn Sie etwas verbessern, das in der Dimension, in der das Tool verwendet wurde, bereits existiert, ist das Marktrisiko normalerweise sehr gering. Es ist so, als ob wir für dieses Tool bezahlen, weil es uns fünf Minuten spart. Eine Möglichkeit zur Risikominderung besteht darin, sich auf Dimensionen zu konzentrieren, bei denen bereits nachgewiesen ist, dass in dieser Dimension Verbesserungsbedarf besteht. Prototyping ist der neue Zauberer hinter dem Bildschirm. Die Entwicklung des KI-Ökosystems bietet eine interessante Chance. Wenn Sie sich Vibe-Coding oder sogar Dinge ansehen, die kein Vibe-Coding sind, gibt es so viele Möglichkeiten, Prototypen zu erstellen und vorläufige Versionen von Dingen zu erstellen, die funktionieren. Sie beweisen nicht, dass sie aus technologischer Sicht machbar sind, und sie werden auch nicht unbedingt jemals Produktionscode sein, aber sie sind die neue Version des Wizard of Oz-Tests. Die alte Version war ein Mensch hinter dem Bildschirm, der dafür sorgte, dass die Dinge funktionierten. Die neue Version ist ChatGPT oder Claude mit etwas Kaugummi und Kleber und ein paar Eingabeaufforderungen, und alles funktioniert, und wir können einige Dinge sehr kostengünstig beweisen. Wenn diese Dinge funktionieren, können wir daraus eine robustere Lösung machen. Nehmen Sie den Binnenmarkt ernst Zu dieser Erkenntnis komme ich immer wieder zurück: Es gibt einen Binnenmarkt, und Sie müssen ihn wie einen Markt behandeln, auf dem die Menschen Optionen haben. Selbst wenn wir Aufzeichnungssysteme entwickeln, ist es wichtig, wie Menschen sie verwenden. Ihr CRM ist ein Aufzeichnungssystem, aber werden die Leute diese oder jene Funktion wirklich nutzen oder werden sie nur das Nötigste tun, um damit durchzukommen? Wir müssen die Produktmanagement- und Produkterkennungstechniken auch auf den Binnenmarkt anwenden. Die Menschen haben die Wahl, die Produkte, die wir für sie entwickeln, intern zu verwenden, aber sie haben auch die Wahl, dies nicht zu tun. Wie Clemens es ausdrückte: Wenn sie Ihr glänzendes, großartiges Tool nicht verwenden, lohnt es sich vielleicht, sich damit zu befassen und es so zu behandeln: „Wir bekommen einen schlechten NPS, lasst uns ein paar Benutzerinterviews machen.“ Oder wir sehen keine Nutzung, also schauen wir uns die Piratenkennzahlen intern an. Kennen die Leute unser Tool? Aktivieren sie? Nutzen sie es nach der Aktivierung tatsächlich? Benutzen sie es weiterhin? Bezahlen sie dafür? Letzteres ist das Interessante, da die Leute intern normalerweise für nichts bezahlen. Woher wissen Sie also, dass die Leute tatsächlich bereit sind, in dieses Tool zu investieren? Vielleicht reicht es aus, dass sie ihre Zeit als Ersatz für Geld investieren. Vielleicht werden wir irgendwann sehen, dass Leute für die Nutzung von KI-Tokens bezahlen: Sind sie wirklich bereit, für den KI-Verbrauch der Werkzeuge ihrer Abteilung zu zahlen? Clemens wies darauf hin, wo dieses Experiment bereits läuft: Es ist interessant im Entwicklerbereich, wo Entwickler bekanntermaßen billig sind, wenn es um Werkzeuge geht. Aber bei Claude Code und Cursor und diesem und jenem geben alle Geld aus, auch wenn es nicht vom Arbeitgeber erstattet wird, weil sie einfach so viel Wert darin sehen, was die Tools für sie tun. Ich denke immer noch, dass das Unternehmen für das Tool bezahlen sollte, aber es wäre ein interessantes Gedankenexperiment: Wenn wir Ihnen dieses Tool wegnehmen würden, wie viel würden Sie bezahlen, um es zurückzubekommen? Das bezieht sich auf die Frage der Produkt-Markt-Fit-Umfrage. Wie unzufrieden wären Sie, wenn wir Ihnen dieses Tool wegnehmen würden? Wenn wir die KI-Funktionen Ihres CRM wegnehmen würden, wie unzufrieden wären Sie, oder wären Sie eigentlich sehr froh? Das kenne ich aus meiner eigenen Umgebung. Nur wenige Leute, die Agilitätsumwandlungen durchführen, sind bereit, die Teams, mit denen sie zusammenarbeiten, zu fragen: Sind wir ein Hüter? Würden Sie dafür kämpfen, den Prozess, das Betriebssystem, weiterhin zu nutzen? Würden Sie dafür kämpfen, weiterhin auf uns als internen Beratungsdienst zugreifen zu können? items.origTitle: How to Get AI Initiatives Beyond the Proof of Concept
items.origSummary: Originally published on yuvalyeret.com . Where do AI initiatives actually go to die? I’m tempted to say an AI-native CRM that doesn’t require the salespeople to enter information manually, that’s great. Everybody’s gonna love that. But I’ve seen so often that even these obvious assumptions eventually fall flat. How often do we think things are really desirable, a field of dreams that people will really come, and we jump to the technology feasibility? Even for great ideas, do we want to test them? And how do you test something like this without building it in the AI world? Will anybody actually want it once you build it? Clemens Adolphs, co-founder of AIce Labs, in our Scaling with Agility conversation: With everything you ever build there is that market risk broadly: will anybody actually want it once you build it? And market risk doesn’t necessarily need to mean, oh, you’re building a consumer-facing product and they have to buy it. It could also just be an internal tool that you roll out and you want your people to use, but they don’t use it. There’s too much friction. They’d just rather copy paste from ChatGPT than click through your five layers of internal whatever. On his last big project: Let’s say the last big project: it already had some internal validation, because they had a basic tool that did the thing and that had adoption. If you’re improving on something that already exists along the dimension that tool was being used, then that typically has very low market risk. It’s like, oh, we’re paying for this tool because it saves us five minutes. One way to de-risk is go along dimensions where it’s already proven that there is demand for improvement in that dimension. Prototyping is the new wizard behind the screen There’s an interesting opportunity in how the AI ecosystem is evolving. If you look at vibe coding, or even things that aren’t vibe coding, there are so many opportunities to prototype, to create preliminary versions of things that work. They’re not proving feasibility from a technology perspective and they’re not necessarily going to be production code ever, but they’re the new version of the Wizard of Oz test. The old version was a human behind the screen making things work. The new version is ChatGPT or Claude with some gum and glue and a few prompts, and things work, and we can prove some things very cheaply. If those things work, we can make it a more robust solution. Take the internal market seriously Here’s the realization I keep coming back to: you have an internal market, and you need to treat it like a market, where people have options. Even when we are developing systems of record, how people use them matters. Your CRM is a system of record, but are people really going to use this feature or that feature, or are they going to do the minimum they have to in order to get away with it? We need to apply the product management and product discovery techniques to the internal market as well. People have a choice to use the products we’re building for them internally, and they also have a choice not to. As Clemens put it, if they’re not using your shiny awesome tool, maybe it’s worth digging into that and treating it as “we’re getting a bad NPS, let’s do some user interviews.” Or we’re not seeing usage, so let’s look at the pirate metrics internally. Are people aware of our tool? Are they activating? Once they’re activating, are they actually using it? Do they continue using it? Are they paying for it? That last one is the interesting one, because internally people don’t typically pay for anything. So how do you know people are actually willing to invest in that tool? Maybe it’s enough that they invest their time as a replacement for money. Maybe at some point we’ll see people paying for AI tokens for usage: are they really willing to pay for the AI consumption of their department’s tooling? Clemens pointed at where that experiment is already running: It’s interesting in the developer space, where famously developers are cheap when it comes to tooling. But with Claude Code and Cursor and this and that, everybody is shelling out money even if it’s not reimbursed by the employer, because they just see so much value in what the tools do for them. I still think the business should pay for the tool, but it would be an interesting thought experiment: if we took this tool away from you, how much would you pay to get it back? That relates to the product-market-fit survey question. How dissatisfied would you be if we took this tool away from you? If we took away the AI capabilities on your CRM, how unhappy would you be, or would you actually be very glad? I know that from my own space. Few people running agility transformations are willing to ask the teams they work with: are we a keeper? Would you fight to keep using the process, the operating system? Would you fight to keep having access to us as an internal consulting service? If you’re an internal consultant, whether that’s an AI…

items.origTitle: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
items.origSummary: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. items.title: KI-gestützte Verfeinerungsvorbereitung und das Risiko, wenn aus einem Vorschlag eine Entscheidung wird
items.summary: TL; DR: Der Product Backlog Refinement Agent und das Risiko, wenn aus einem Vorschlag eine Entscheidung wird. Die Vorbereitung einer Verfeinerungssitzung ist mühsam, und KI ist im mühsamen Teil gut: Sie liest jeden Product Backlog-Eintrag, jede wiederholte Kommentarspalte und die eigenen Aufzeichnungen des Teams am Nachmittag zuvor. Das Risiko liegt woanders. Ein Verfeinerungsagent, der gebeten wird, „bei der Verfeinerung zu helfen“, kann dem Team die Diskussion entziehen, ohne ein einziges Akzeptanzkriterium zu schreiben: Es reicht aus, dem Produktbesitzer oder Produktmanager „vorzuschlagen“, welche Elemente geschlossen, zusammengeführt, geteilt oder erstellt werden sollen, und die Fragen, die das Team ausarbeiten sollte, landen bereits im Briefing. Die Abhilfe ist eine vor dem ersten Durchlauf festgelegte Grenze: Der Agent markiert Beweise und stellt Fragen, der Product Owner prüft das Briefing und legt die Agenda fest, und das Team verfeinert. Wenn Sie diese Grenze zusammen mit dem, was der Agent liest und wer seine Ausgabe überprüft, in einen A3-Handoff-Canvas schreiben, wird aus einer guten Absicht eine Regel, die der Agent befolgt und die der Product Owner überprüfen kann. Bildthese: In diesem Artikel wird erklärt, wie Produktbesitzer und Produktmanager KI nutzen können, um die Verfeinerung des Product Backlogs vorzubereiten, ohne der Diskussion im Team zuvorzukommen: vier Beweisprüfungen, ein vierteiliger Test, der Vorschläge von Entscheidungen trennt, schriftliche Grenzen und menschliche Überprüfung des Briefings des Agenten. Haftungsausschluss: Ich habe vor Jahrzehnten Charniak/McDermotts Buch über „Künstliche Intelligenz“ gelesen; Natürlich verwende ich KI für Recherchen, Übersetzungen, Korrekturlesen, herausfordernde Handlungsstränge und Artikelstrukturen sowie für die Erstellung von Artefakten wie Grafiken und Zusammenfassungen. Es ist ein Produktionswerkzeug, kein Ersatz für das Denken. 🗞 Soll ich Sie über Artikel wie diesen benachrichtigen? Eindrucksvoll! Sie können sich hier für den Newsletter „Food for Agile Thought“ anmelden und sich den über 35.000 Abonnenten anschließen. Die Gefahr, dass aus einer Vorbereitung eine Entscheidung wird. Die bekannte Sorge um KI bei der Verfeinerung des Product Backlogs besteht darin, dass ein Modell die Product Backlog-Elemente, die Akzeptanzkriterien und die Schätzungen schreibt und ein müdes Team sie an einem Dienstagnachmittag durchnickt. Die Sorge ist berechtigt; Es beschreibt jedoch den einfachen Fall, da ein ausgearbeitetes Akzeptanzkriterium sichtbar ist und ein Team normalerweise bemerken würde, dass jemand anderes seine Hausaufgaben gemacht hat. Der anspruchsvollere Fall scheint Hilfe zu sein. Stellen Sie sich ein hypothetisches Briefing eines Refinement-Agenten vor, das keine Beschreibungen, keine Akzeptanzkriterien und keinen neuen Auftrag enthält, aber dennoch empfiehlt, ein Element als Duplikat zu schließen, ein anderes aufzuteilen, ein drittes zu erstellen und vier Elemente als „bereite Kandidaten“ für den nächsten Sprint zu bezeichnen. Jede Zeile liest sich wie ein freundlicher Rat an den Product Owner, und jede Zeile klärt eine Frage, bevor das Team sie besprochen hat. Eine Empfehlung entscheidet nichts, bis jemand sie akzeptiert und danach handelt. Sobald es jedoch auf der Tagesordnung steht, diskutiert das Team wahrscheinlich die Empfehlung und nicht die Frage dahinter, und so wird aus der Vorbereitung still und leise eine Entscheidung. Es schleicht sich durch die Hintertür ein und nährt sich vom menschlichen Wunsch, unnötige Arbeit zu vermeiden, wenn der organisatorische Druck ohnehin schon hoch ist. Wozu die Verfeinerung dient und worauf bei der Vorbereitung verzichtet werden sollte Der Scrum-Leitfaden beschreibt die Verfeinerung als „eine fortlaufende Aktivität, bei der Details wie eine Beschreibung, Reihenfolge und Größe hinzugefügt werden“, die die Mechanik erfasst und den Zweck außer Acht lässt. Ich betrachte die Verfeinerung als den letzten Teil der Produktfindung, sobald die Hypothesenvalidierung etabliert ist: Das Team fragt, ob ein Artikel wirklich die beste Nutzung seiner Zeit ist oder ob etwas anderes mehr Wert für die Kunden schaffen würde. Ein Product Backlog-Eintrag ist ein Zeichen für diese Diskussion, eine Einladung zur Abstimmung, und eine gute Sitzung endet mit einem gemeinsamen Verständnis, das ausreicht, um die nächste Investitionsentscheidung zu treffen, einschließlich der Entscheidung, nichts zu bauen. Viele Teams veranstalten hierfür eine regelmäßige Sitzung, und oft werden diese Sitzungen zu einer Suche nach Problemen, die jemand am Tag zuvor hätte erkennen können: ein Punkt, den ein Stakeholder unbedingt an die Spitze verschieben möchte, ein Rückstandspunkt ohne Akzeptanzkriterien, von dem jeder erwartet hat, dass jemand anderes ihn schreibt, ein Punkt, den seit sechs Monaten niemand mehr berührt hat. Es gibt Vorbereitungen, um dem Team diese Art von Verwaltungsarbeit zu ersparen, und das Lesen eines Jira-Exports und der Notizen des Teams am Nachmittag zuvor ist genau die Art gründlicher, mühsamer Arbeit, die ein KI-Agent gut erledigt. Die Frage ist, wo die Vorbereitung endet. Im September habe ich zehn Anti-Patterns beschrieben, die schlimmer werden, wenn Teams KI zu einem dysfunktionalen Product-Backlog-Prozess hinzufügen, darunter „Refinement Without the Team“, und ein Assistent, der dem Product Owner vorgefertigte Lösungen überreicht, ist eine höfliche Version dieses Anti-Patterns: Das Team trifft sich immer noch, doch die Entscheidungen, die es treffen sollte, treffen bereits vorgefertigt ein. Meiner Ansicht nach ist die schwerwiegendste Konsequenz einer dysfunktionalen Verfeinerung, dass ein Team seine Fähigkeit zum produktiven Diskurs verliert. Typischerweise folgt daraus, dass man das Falsche baut; Denken Sie an mangelnde Kapitalrendite und Opportunitätskosten. Also meine Regel für so etwas...
items.origTitle: AI-Assisted Refinement Preparation and the Risk When a Suggestion Becomes a Decision
items.origSummary: TL; DR: The Product Backlog Refinement Agent and the Risk When a Suggestion Becomes a Decision Preparing a refinement session is tedious, and AI is good at the tedious part: reading every Product Backlog item, every repeated comment column, and the team’s own records on the afternoon before. The risk sits elsewhere. A refinement agent asked to “help with refinement” can take the conversation away from the team without writing a single acceptance criterion: “suggesting” to the Product Owner or Product Manager which items to close, merge, split, or create is enough, and the questions the team was supposed to work out arrive in the brief already answered. The remedy is a boundary decided before the first run: the agent marks evidence and asks questions, the Product Owner checks the brief and sets the agenda, and the team refines. Writing that boundary into an A3 Handoff Canvas, together with what the agent reads and who checks its output, turns a good intention into a rule the agent follows and the Product Owner can verify. Image Thesis : This article explains how Product Owners and Product Managers can use AI to prepare Product Backlog refinement without pre-empting the team’s conversation: four evidence checks, a four-part test separating suggestions from decisions, written boundaries, and human verification of the agent’s brief. Disclaimer : I read Charniak/McDermott’s book on “Artificial Intelligence” decades ago; of course, I use AI for research, translations, proofreading, challenging story arcs and article structures, creating artifacts such as graphics, and summarization. It is a production tool, not a substitute for thinking. 🗞 Shall I notify you about articles like this one? Awesome! You can sign up here for the ‘Food for Agile Thought’ newsletter and join 35,000-plus subscribers . The Danger of a Preparation Turning Into a Decision The familiar worry about AI in Product Backlog refinement is that a model writes the Product Backlog items, the acceptance criteria, and the estimates, and a tired team nods them through on a Tuesday afternoon. The worry is justified; however, it describes the easy case, because a drafted acceptance criterion is visible, and a team would usually notice that someone else did its homework. The more challenging case looks like help. Consider a hypothetical brief by a refinement agent that contains no descriptions, no acceptance criteria, and no new order, yet recommends closing one item as a duplicate, splitting another, creating a third, and calling four items “ready candidates” for the next Sprint. Every line reads as friendly advice to the Product Owner, and every line settles a question before the team has discussed it. A recommendation decides nothing until someone accepts it and acts on it. Once it sits on the agenda, however, the team is likely to discuss the recommendation instead of the question behind it, and that is how preparation quietly turns into a decision. It sneaks in through the back door, feeding on the human desire to avoid unnecessary work when organizational pressure is already high. What Refinement Is For, and What Preparation Should Leave Alone The Scrum Guide describes refinement as “an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size,” which captures the mechanics and leaves out the purpose. I see refinement as the final part of product discovery, once hypothesis validation has been established: the team asks whether an item is really the best use of its time or whether something else would create more value for customers. A Product Backlog item is a token for that discussion, an invitation to align, and a good session ends with shared understanding sufficient to make the next investment decision, including the decision not to build something. Many teams hold a regular session for this, and often those sessions turn into a hunt for problems someone could have spotted the day before: an item a stakeholder insists on moving to the top, a backlog item without acceptance criteria that everyone expected someone else to write, an item nobody has touched for 6 months. Preparation exists to spare the team that kind of administrative work, and reading a Jira export and the team’s notes on the afternoon before is exactly the kind of thorough, tedious work an AI agent does well. The question is where preparation ends. In September, I described ten anti-patterns that get worse when teams add AI to a dysfunctional Product Backlog process , “Refinement Without the Team” among them, and an assistant that hands the Product Owner ready-made resolutions is a polite version of that anti-pattern: the team still meets, yet the decisions it was supposed to reach already arrive pre-made. In my view, the most critical consequence of dysfunctional refinement is a team that loses its ability to have productive discourse. items.title: Feature-Factorys nennen sich selbst nicht Feature-Factorys
items.summary: Image Sprint Reviews reveal the operating model within twenty minutes. I have been sitting in them across industries since 2010, and the tell is consistent: what the room celebrates. Teams that function as feature factories present a list of completed features, stakeholders check things off, and nobody asks whether any of it landed with users. Done means deployed, and deployed means done. That pattern has a name, and it is more common than the number of companies that would accept the label. Three Numbers That Belong Together Atlassian surveyed more than 1,000 product professionals across the US and Europe for their first State of Product report in 2026 [1]. Eighty-five percent of respondents feel empowered to lead or influence product strategy and innovation. And yet 84 percent are concerned the products they are currently working on will not succeed in the market. More striking: only 12 percent name driving measurable business results as one of the most rewarding aspects of their work. It ranks last in the survey, below collaboration, problem-solving, user insight, innovation, and shaping product vision. Teams that feel strategically empowered but fear their products will fail, and find driving results the least rewarding part of the job, are describing a single condition: influence without accountability for what happens after the work ships. What the Structure Reveals The same report explains why. Eighty percent of product teams do not involve engineers in ideation, problem definition, or roadmap creation [1]. Engineers arrive during concept validation or after design is finalized. The structure assigns discovery to one group and execution to another. This is not a calendar problem or a communication gap. It is a structural choice about who participates in what. When engineers are brought in to estimate and build rather than to understand and discover, the team has already decided what to solve. The only open question is how quickly it can be delivered. John Cutler coined the phrase "feature factory" to describe this pattern [2]. Marty Cagan draws the same line differently: a feature team is handed a solution and ships it. An empowered team is handed a problem and owns whether it worked [3]. Both descriptions point at the same organizational design. A team accountable for delivery is not the same as a team accountable for outcomes, and the incentives that follow from each are entirely different. The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack names the gap in the artifact itself: output done means the increment built successfully; outcome done means the business outcome was achieved [4]. Feature factories have a clear definition for the first. The second is not missing because nobody thought of it. It is missing because the accountability structure assigns results somewhere else. The 12 percent finding becomes legible in that frame. In a feature factory, results are downstream of decisions the team did not make. The market's response belongs to sales, to marketing, or to conditions outside the team's control. Results cannot be what makes the work rewarding when the operating model places them outside the team's responsibility. The most rewarding aspects of product work, according to the same survey, are collaboration, problem-solving, and user insight. A feature factory can provide all three. Teams run discovery, collaborate with engineers on how to build something, talk to users. The operating model does not remove those satisfactions. What it removes is accountability for what the product does after it ships. The 12 percent figure follows directly from that. What the Signals Look Like The pattern is not hard to spot, though it does not announce itself. Stakeholders bring wireframes and feature specifications to planning sessions, not problems. The team's job is to estimate and build. There is no question to discover the answer to. Sprint Reviews show what shipped. The room applauds. Nobody presents data on what changed for users since the previous Sprint, because the operating model does not require that data to exist. Velocity is tracked as performance: teams are asked to maintain or increase their rate. Velocity measures throughput, not value. When it functions as a performance indicator rather than a flow signal, it trains the team to go faster rather than to be more selective. The definition of done stops at deployment: the feature is live, the ticket is closed, and the Scrum Team is already planning the next cycle. The Atlassian data puts a number on it: only 31 percent of product teams make rapid experimentation and iteration part of their regular process [1]. The other 69 percent ship and move on, which is what a delivery-first model produces. A Fair Objection Ben Erez made a careful argument that feature factories suit some companies [2]. When a CEO has a clear, compelling product vision, or when the goal is competitive feature parity, teams that execute well against a defined roadmap deliver real value.…

items.origTitle: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
items.origSummary: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it.

items.title: Eine mediterrane Ernährung kann die Produktion winziger Proteine fördern, die Herz und Gehirn schützen
items.summary: Wissenschaftler haben einen überraschenden neuen Hinweis darauf entdeckt, warum die Mittelmeerdiät so gut für Herz, Gehirn und gesundes Altern ist. Forscher am USC fanden heraus, dass ältere Erwachsene, die sich genau an die Diät hielten, einen höheren Gehalt an zwei winzigen Proteinen hatten, Humanin und SHMOOSE, die von den Mitochondrien, den energieproduzierenden Strukturen in den Zellen, produziert werden. Diese Proteine ​​werden mit dem Schutz vor Herzerkrankungen, Alzheimer und altersbedingten Schäden in Verbindung gebracht.
items.origTitle: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
items.origSummary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

items.title: AI... Improving the Wrong System Faster
items.summary: Many management AI conversation drift to the same place fast. Which model? Where can we automate? How much faster can developers code? Which admin tasks can we cut? Useful questions. But they aren't yet organizational design questions and that's exactly why most AI programs stall. When you add AI onto the existing organization, the wheels spin faster, but are you heading in the right direction?. The new Death march Back in the day there was this idea of software factories, and of-course it did not work as development is not production. Then agile development became popular and sadly 30 years later here we are again…Orgs are building software factories, but now with AI tools, agents, sprints, backlogs, planning events, all in place… Likely we will get similar problems, no not death marches anymore, but more subtle things like: Mountains of generated code nobody understands. Features delivered faster than anyone can validate their value. Architectural complexity accumulating at machine speed. Management mistaking agent productivity for organizational effectiveness. Why? Well, i think software development is still not production. The hard part of software development was never typing code. ( coding is to development what typing is to writing ) It was understanding the problem, discovering what works, making design decisions, and dealing with uncertainty. AI makes producing code super fast and cheap. So, when you organize AI agents into software factories, you optimizing exactly the wrong thing: output. More features. More code. More tickets completed. More velocity. Lol 😅 What about solving the right problems the right way. Automating business processes has a different challenge Automating waste creation just makes?.... yes more waste faster. Don't automate waste before asking why the waste exists in the first place! If a request goes through many handoffs, sits in approval queues, and bounces between silos, AI will not fix the anything. Instead, it accelerates a broken system to become more broken. Reminds me of a famous quite from John Seddon "Agile... making the wrong things faster". Inspired by that thinking, I've coined my own version for the AI era: "AI... improving the wrong system faster" You get faster handoffs into the same bottleneck. Lower unit cost per step, same end-to-end delay, same frustrated customer. These are just the same problems org-designers have been working for decades. Improving a step without considering the design that includes that step is a local optimization. As CAO puts it: adding tooling (or now, agents) might ease the pain temporarily, but it won't change the fact that the system is built to produce slow, brittle work. Want different results? Change the system. What AI actually changes: the economics of dividing work Organizations divide work for two reasons. Complexity: the work is too broad or deep for one person or team, so we create specialists, handoffs, review layers, support functions. Power: some decisions shouldn't sit in one place, so we create boundaries for governance, control, risk, and audit. Almost all of our specialization came from the first reason. And that's precisely the reason AI erodes. Twenty years ago a UI change passed designer → frontend → backend → tester → operations, every handoff adding delay, misunderstanding, and rework. Now a few capable people, supported by AI, can move much further across that chain themselves. Not perfectly, not always alone, but far more than before. AI lets a person or team contain more of the work. This is not about productivity but a shift in the economics of how we divide work. Which means the boundaries you drew to manage complexity may no longer be worth their coordination cost. The real improvements are not in faster tasks; instead, they are in a changed work boundary. So considerer the boundary, don't waste your time in the old one. When AI lets a team own more of the outcome, the design should follow: Product Groups can get broader and more autonomous — they contain more of what used to require other units. Dependencies created by fragmented capability become unnecessary — remove them, don't automate them. Shared services can shift from ticket queues to enabling systems — stop being a gatekeeper teams wait on; become a platform teams build on. Image Figure 1. Product group redesign example in CAO Studio. The best AI use cases aren't isolated productivity improvements. Instead, they let an organizational unit own more of the work required to improve its outcome. In developments this might be: discovery, research synthesis, documentation, testing, dependency analysis, routine coordination. The ones that fail are the ones that hide accountability, bypass necessary controls, or keep the system as is. Keep the boundaries that exist to constrain power One hard line. AI reduces the boundaries created by the limits of capability. It does not remove the boundaries created by the need to constrain power. Governance,…
